withdraw_bank.prompt: Your machine has more than one python3 installed. One command lists every python3 your shell can find, in the order it searches, instead of only the first. Write that one command.
withdraw_bank.explain: which -a python3 lists every match, in search order. which python3 prints only the first one, and the first one is the one that runs.

withdraw_bank.prompt: The shell looks through a list of folders, in order, to find the program you typed, and runs the first match it finds. Name that list. One word.
withdraw_bank.explain: The list is PATH. The shell searches its folders in order and runs the first match, which is how two installs of the same program can both be present while only one of them ever runs.

withdraw_bank.prompt: One command asks the machine itself which architecture it is — not which architecture a Python was built for. Write that one command.
withdraw_bank.explain: uname -m reports the machine’s own architecture. platform.machine() reports what the running Python was built for, and on this machine the two answers can differ.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Write the one command that creates a virtual environment in a folder named .venv inside the folder you are in now.
withdraw_bank.explain: python3 -m venv .venv builds the environment with the python3 that runs the command, and the environment keeps that Python. It does not go looking for a newer or a native one. It has to be python3, not python: they are two different names, and on your Mac the shell finds nothing called python until an environment is switched on. The environment you are making is not on yet, so python -m venv .venv stops with command not found.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Write the one command that prints the folder you are in now.
withdraw_bank.explain: pwd prints the folder you are in — the folder your next command will act in.

withdraw_bank.prompt: SQL’s SUM(amount) works over a set, and gives the same answer however the rows are arranged. The question “which row did the running total first pass 50 on” needs something a set does not have. Name it. One word.
withdraw_bank.explain: It needs an order. A running total depends on the sequence the rows arrive in, so “the first row to cross 50” has no answer until the rows are in an order.

withdraw_bank.prompt: You are in a loop over rows and the row you were looking for has been found. One keyword leaves the loop immediately, without touching the rows that are left. One word.
withdraw_bank.explain: break leaves the loop at once, so the rows after it are never looked at. That is how you report the first row that meets a condition rather than the last one.

withdraw_bank.prompt: You are looking at one row at a time, and only some of the rows interest you. One keyword runs the lines under it only when something is true, and skips them otherwise. One word.
withdraw_bank.explain: if runs the lines under it only when what you asked about that row is true. It is how one row out of six is acted on and the other five are passed over.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A list is held in a name called rows. Write the first line of a loop that takes its rows one at a time, holding each one in a name called row. One line of code.
withdraw_bank.explain: for row in rows: starts the loop. The lines under it run once for each row, in the order the list holds them, and row holds a different row each time round.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Python has no brackets to mark where a loop’s body starts and ends. What is done to the lines of the body so that Python knows they belong to the loop? One word.
withdraw_bank.explain: Indentation. The lines of the body are pushed in by the same amount under the line that starts the loop. The first line that is not pushed in is no longer part of the body.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A name called price holds a number. Write the piece of code that asks whether price is more than 100. One short piece of code.
withdraw_bank.explain: price > 100 asks a question whose answer is True or False. Written after if, it decides whether the lines under the if run or are skipped.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A single = gives a name a value. Write the symbol Python uses to ask whether two values are equal instead.
withdraw_bank.explain: == asks whether two values are equal, and the answer is True or False. A single = asks nothing: it gives the name on its left the value on its right.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A virtual environment already exists in a folder named .venv inside the folder you are in now. Write the one command that switches your shell to it.
withdraw_bank.explain: source .venv/bin/activate switches this shell to the environment. It puts the environment’s own folder first in PATH, so from then on python3 finds the environment’s Python before any other.

withdraw_bank.prompt: One command asks the machine which architecture it is. A Python can be asked a different question: what architecture was it built for? Write the short piece of Python code that answers it. It starts with platform.
withdraw_bank.explain: platform.machine() reports the architecture the running Python was built for. That can differ from what the machine says about itself, which is why the two are asked separately.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A Python file named report.py is in the folder you are in now. Write the one command that runs it.
withdraw_bank.explain: python3 report.py hands the file to Python, which runs its lines from the top down. python3 is a name your shell has to look up, and the first match it finds is the one that runs the file. python is a different name: on your Mac only a switched-on environment supplies it, so outside one python report.py stops with command not found. python3 works with or without an environment.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Write the one command that lists what is in the folder you are in now.
withdraw_bank.explain: ls lists what is in the folder you are in. pwd says which folder that is; ls says what it holds.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A folder named cs-core sits in your home folder. Write the one command that moves your shell into it, from wherever you are now.
withdraw_bank.explain: cd ~/cs-core changes the folder you are in. ~ stands for your home folder, so the command works from anywhere. Nothing is printed when it works; pwd shows where you landed.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Write the one command that makes a new, empty folder named data inside the folder you are in now.
withdraw_bank.explain: mkdir data makes the folder and leaves you where you were. It does not move you into it: that is what cd is for.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A small text file named notes.txt is in the folder you are in now. Write the one command that prints what is in it to the screen.
withdraw_bank.explain: cat notes.txt prints the file’s contents under your command and changes nothing in it. It is how you read the small file inside an environment that says which Python made it.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Inside a virtual environment’s folder sits a small text file that says which Python the environment was made from. Name that file.
withdraw_bank.explain: pyvenv.cfg, at the top of the environment’s folder. Its home line names the folder of the Python that made the environment, and its version line names that Python’s version.

withdraw_bank.prompt: Two Pythons are installed, 3.12 and 3.15. The python3 your shell finds first is the 3.12 one, and you make a virtual environment with it. With the environment switched on, which version does its Python report? Answer with the first two numbers, like 3.xx.
withdraw_bank.explain: 3.12. An environment keeps the Python that made it; it does not go looking for the newest one on the machine. To get 3.15 inside an environment, make the environment with the 3.15 Python.

withdraw_bank.prompt: A program starts with import sys. Write the short piece of code that gives the path of the Python that is running the program. It starts with sys.
withdraw_bank.explain: sys.executable is the path of the Python running the program. With an environment switched on, it points inside .venv: that is how a program can say which Python ran it.

variants.ask: A list called orders holds four numbers, in this order: 5, 9, 2, 7. A loop runs for order in orders. The loop body is exactly two lines, in this order: first biggest = 0, then if order > biggest: biggest = order. There is nothing else in the body, and nothing is set before the loop. After the loop ends, print(biggest) runs. What does it show?
options: 9 — the largest of the four orders.
7 — the last order, because the body sets biggest back to 0 on every round.
0 — because biggest = 0 sits inside the loop, and the loop finishes by running it one last time.
variants.explain: The body runs once per order, so biggest = 0 runs four times. Each round compares one order against 0 and keeps it, so at the end the name holds the last order, not the largest. A number that has to last the whole loop must be set before the loop starts.

variants.ask: A function takes two things and returns nothing. Its body is exactly two lines. First: label = label.upper(), where .upper() hands back an upper-case copy of the text and changes nothing. Then: notes.append("checked"), which adds an item to the list it was given. The caller sets name = "ana" and log = [], calls the function with name and log, and then prints name and log. What does the print show?
options: ANA and ['checked'] — the function changed both of the things it was given.
ana and [] — it changed neither, because a function only ever works on its own copies.
ana and ['checked'] — the list changed and the text did not.
variants.explain: Assigning to label points the function’s own name at a new string, and the caller’s name still points at the old one. append changes the one list both names point at, so the caller sees it straight away. What crosses out of a function is what you return, plus anything you changed in place.
